method: Apps were chosen from the user-named list plus the highest-starred additions found in the sources, then ranked by the strongest usage figure available (use measures first: W3Techs share, registered sites, survey counts; then GitHub stars), interleaving by judgement where only different measures exist. Each app was decomposed into capabilities and each capability into pure TypeScript blocks, existing blocks first. The first ten rebuilds were fixed by value times coverage; the remaining new blocks were then ordered greedily: repeatedly complete the app with the highest rank weight (1 over rank) per missing block, adding its dependencies first. Priority 1 is the first-ten set, priority 2 completes the 300-block mark, priority 3 is the rest.

firstTen.name: Vaultwarden
firstTen.why: It guards the most sensitive data a person owns, its server surface is small, and the wire protocol is fixed by official clients, so every behaviour can be compared byte for byte with a reference.
missing: Mobile push relay (provider interface and twin only)
Duo, YubiKey cloud and other third-party second factors (interface and twin only)
firstTen.reference: The Vaultwarden server and the official Bitwarden server API, exercised by the official Bitwarden command-line client and browser extension through the oracle block.
firstTen.what: A server for a password manager. People keep logins, cards, notes and keys in an encrypted vault that their phone, browser and desktop apps share. The server stores and syncs the vault but cannot read it, because the apps encrypt everything before it leaves the device.
firstTen.who: Individuals, families and small teams who self-host; the most favoured password manager in the 2025 self-hosting survey.

firstTen.name: Uptime Kuma
firstTen.why: Almost every product needs uptime checks and a status page, the checks are well defined, and it exercises probes, alert rules and public pages that every other rebuild reuses.
missing: ICMP ping and other raw-socket probes (provider interface; the runtime supplies the socket)
Most of the 90 or so notification providers (each is an adapter over api-client)
firstTen.reference: Uptime Kuma 2.x: its monitor semantics, socket events, status page JSON and badge output.
firstTen.what: A monitor that checks websites, servers and services on a schedule, alerts people when one fails, and publishes status pages.
firstTen.who: Self-hosters, small teams and agencies that want to know before their customers do.

firstTen.name: Umami
firstTen.why: Analytics is a universal need, the data model is simple, and it reuses ingest, rollups and charts that every dashboard product needs.
missing: The browser tracker script (a UI asset, not a block)
IP-to-place data files (licensed data, supplied at deploy time)
Database back ends beyond the store the factory generates
firstTen.reference: Umami's collection and statistics API, compared by replaying the same event stream into both.
firstTen.what: Privacy-first web analytics. A small script on a site sends page views and events; the server counts visitors, sessions, sources, funnels and retention without cookies or personal data.
firstTen.who: Site owners, product teams and agencies that want analytics without a consent banner or a data broker.

firstTen.name: Listmonk
firstTen.why: Email at volume is hard to get right, costs real money on hosted services, and the same blocks serve receipts, digests and marketing automation.
missing: POP3 bounce mailbox polling (a thin addition to imap-protocol)
firstTen.reference: listmonk's REST API and its template functions, compared on the same subscriber and campaign fixtures.
firstTen.what: A mailing-list and newsletter server: people subscribe, an editor writes a campaign, and the server sends it in throttled batches and tracks bounces and clicks.
firstTen.who: Publishers, nonprofits and product teams that send their own newsletters instead of paying per subscriber.

firstTen.name: Cal.com
firstTen.why: Booking is a daily-use product with a sharp definition of correct: no double bookings, correct across time zones and daylight-saving changes. The library already holds the time and booking cores.
missing: Google and Microsoft calendar provider connections (adapters over api-client and credential-vault)
Payment provider apps beyond the provider interface
firstTen.reference: Cal.com's availability and bookings API (its slots endpoint), compared across a matrix of zones, buffers and recurring rules.
firstTen.what: Scheduling: a person publishes their availability, others pick a time, and both calendars update with a meeting link and reminders.
firstTen.who: Consultants, sales and support teams, clinics and anyone who sells time.

firstTen.name: Paperless-ngx
firstTen.why: Every organisation drowns in documents; the pipeline (intake, extract, classify, search) is what most document products need.
missing: The OCR engine itself (provider interface and twin; a real engine runs outside)
firstTen.reference: Paperless-ngx's REST API and its matching rules, checked on a corpus of sample documents.
firstTen.what: A document archive. Scans and emails arrive in an inbox, are read by OCR, are filed with tags, correspondents and dates by matching rules, and become searchable.
firstTen.who: Households, accountants and small offices going paperless.

firstTen.name: BookStack
firstTen.why: Documentation is every team's second product; the page tree, revisions and permissions are reused by every knowledge product, and the library already holds history, search and tree.
firstTen.reference: BookStack's REST API and export formats, with its permission model compared page by page.
firstTen.what: A wiki organised as shelves, books, chapters and pages, with a rich editor, revisions, permissions and PDF export.
firstTen.who: Teams and IT departments documenting how things work.

firstTen.name: Documenso
firstTen.why: Signing is high-value and high-trust, the process is a precise state machine, and the sealing and evidence blocks are reused anywhere a record must be provably unchanged.
missing: Qualified electronic signatures from trust service providers
firstTen.reference: Documenso's document and recipient API, with the sealed PDF checked by an independent PDF signature validator.
firstTen.what: Electronic signing. A sender uploads a document, places signature fields, invites signers in order, and receives a sealed PDF with a certificate of completion.
firstTen.who: Small businesses, landlords, freelancers and HR teams that sign contracts every week.

firstTen.name: Keycloak
firstTen.why: Identity is the shared dependency of every other rebuild and has a public conformance suite, so correctness can be proved rather than argued.
missing: Hardware attestation trust stores for passkeys
firstTen.reference: Keycloak itself, plus the OpenID Foundation conformance suite for OpenID Connect.
firstTen.what: An identity server: one place where people sign in once and every application trusts the answer, using OpenID Connect, OAuth 2, SAML, LDAP and passkeys.
firstTen.who: Enterprises, platform teams and every company with more than a handful of internal apps.

firstTen.name: n8n
firstTen.why: It is the most-starred application in the inventory, and its engine (graph, expressions, credentials, retries, run history) is the connective tissue the factory itself needs.
missing: The several hundred integration nodes (each an adapter over node-registry and api-client)
A sandbox for user-written code steps
firstTen.reference: n8n's workflow JSON format and its node execution semantics, run on exported workflows and compared item by item.
firstTen.what: Workflow automation. People draw a graph of triggers and steps that move data between services, and the engine runs it on a schedule, on a webhook, or on demand.
firstTen.who: Operations teams, developers and citizen builders connecting systems without writing integrations.
